Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National Javits funeral service: Use upcoming Thanksgiving gatherings to teach children not to hate – Al Sharpton Source : Kenneth Awotwe Darko 20 November 2026 6:17pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
American civil rights activist Rev. Al Sharpton has urged parents to use Thanksgiving family gatherings to teach their children tolerance, acceptance and respect for people from different backgrounds, following the killing of 15-year-old Ghanaian teenager Badu Nkansah Frimpong, popularly known as Javits.
Delivering the eulogy at Javits’ funeral in the Bronx, New York, on Friday, November 20, Sharpton said growing hostility towards immigrants and people with different accents and places of birth was filtering into the attitudes of young people.
He challenged parents to use the opportunity presented by Thanksgiving, when families traditionally gather for meals, to have conversations with their children about rejecting hatred and embracing others.
Sharpton said the lessons taught at home were important in confronting prejudice and divisions among young people.
His appeal formed part of a broader call for African Americans and African immigrants to recognise their shared heritage and work together against intolerance and violence.
“We are all African, some displaced African, some at home African, we're all African,” he said.
He expressed concern that hostility towards people because of their accents or countries of birth had become a source of division, warning that the prejudice was affecting children.
The civil rights activist also called on the African American community to show greater solidarity with African immigrants, saying the response to violence should not depend on the background of the victim or those involved.
Although he acknowledged that the full circumstances surrounding Javits’ killing were not yet established, he said the consequences of the violence required a collective response.
“We don't know all the facts that led to this, but we know the result. And the result's got to be addressed by all of us,” he said.
Sharpton drew on the biblical account of Joseph and his brothers to illustrate how jealousy and hostility could develop into destructive behaviour.
He said Javits’ death should prompt communities to confront what he described as self-hatred, anti-immigrant sentiment and divisions among people of African descent.
The teenager was fatally shot in the Bronx on October 29 while walking to school. He had moved from Ghana to the United States in 2025 to join his father and pursue his education.
Sharpton concluded his eulogy by referring to Javits’ ambition to become a doctor, saying that although he would not fulfil that dream in the conventional sense, his death could inspire efforts to heal divisions in the community.
“Javits, even though you never went to medical school, you became a doctor. We're going to use you to heal the community,” he said.
